title: DNS: how a name becomes an address
goal: By the end, you can follow a name lookup from your program through a resolver to the root, top-level and owner's servers, read a DNS message byte by byte, and predict how long a changed or missing name stays wrong in each place that keeps a copy, Java's own cache included.
opening:
Your friend gets a new phone number and posts it in the group chat at 10:00. At 10:30 you tap her name, and a stranger answers. Your phone saved the old number months ago, and nothing told it to change.

Programs meet the same problem. The payments program knows the bank's computer by a name, `api.bank.example`, and has to turn that name into a numeric address before it can connect. The bank moves to a new address at 10:00. At 10:45, payments still go to the old one.

People say a change like that needs time to "propagate", as if something carried it outward. Nothing does. Old copies of the answer sit in several places, each waiting out its own expiry date.

TCP performance: windows, congestion control and Nagle took the address as given. In this lesson, we'll see where it comes from: we'll follow one lookup down the internet's tree of names, read a DNS message byte by byte, and find every place an old answer can hide. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The bank moves `api.bank.example` to a new address at 10:00. Before the change, the name's record said anyone may keep a copy for 3,600 seconds (an hour). The payments program, written in Java with default settings, looked the name up at 09:59 through the company's resolver, the server that looks names up for the company's programs. At the latest, when does a new connection from that program go to the new address?
options: At once: the bank's own name server sends the change to every resolver
At about 11:00, when the resolver's copy runs out, give or take Java's own 30-second copy
After 24 to 48 hours, the usual time for changes to spread
At 10:30, after half the hour
warmup.why: Nothing sends DNS changes anywhere. The resolver copied the old answer at 09:59 and may hand it out until that copy's hour runs out, at about 10:59. Java may then keep its own copy up to 30 seconds longer. "Propagation" is only copies running out at different times, and an hour means an hour, not two days. One more place can hold on longer still: a connection the program opened earlier keeps talking to the old address until it's closed, whatever DNS says. The last section shows both.

sections.h: Reading a name from the right: a tree with many owners
sections.body:
Every computer on the internet is reached by a numeric IP address, such as `104.20.23.154`. People and programs prefer names, such as `example.com`. DNS, the Domain Name System, turns one into the other: a program asks "what's the address of example.com?" and gets back a number.

Why not keep all names in one big table? Nobody could run it: hundreds of millions of names, changed by their owners every minute, asked for billions of times an hour. DNS splits the problem the way the names are split, at the dots.

Read a name from the right. `api.pay.example.com.` ends in an invisible dot, the root. Under the root are the top-level domains (TLDs): `com`, `org`, `uk`, `test`. Under `com` is `example`, and under that, whatever its owner adds. Any point of the tree can be cut off and handed to a different owner, together with everything below it. That piece is a **zone**, and handing it over is a delegation. The root zone is a short list that says who runs each TLD. The `com` zone says who runs each of its hundred-odd million names, and nothing else about them. The `example.com` zone holds the actual addresses of `example.com` and the names under it.

Think of a set of phone books. The first book lists only which book covers each country. Each country's book lists only which book each company keeps. Only the company's own book has the numbers. In DNS, each zone's book is kept by its authoritative servers, the computers that hold the zone's own records. Their answers are the originals; every other answer is a copy. The picture breaks in one way: a printed book is out of date the day it's printed, while a zone's own servers always give the latest answer. Only the copies go stale.

DNS stores everything as resource records (records, for short): a name, a type, a TTL and some data. TTL means time to live, how many seconds anyone may keep a copy. These types cover most of what you'll meet, with real records from this lesson's Try its:

| Type | Holds | Example |
|---|---|---|
| A | an IPv4 address, the common four-number kind | `example.com. 300 A 104.20.23.154` |
| AAAA | an IPv6 address, the longer kind (IPv6 for application engineers) | `example.com. AAAA 2606:4700:10::6814:179a` |
| CNAME | "this name is another name for that one" | `www.wikipedia.org. CNAME dyna.wikimedia.org.` |
| NS | the servers of a zone: a delegation | `example.com. NS hera.ns.cloudflare.com.` |
| SOA | facts about a zone, among them how long to remember a "no" | `iana.org. SOA sns.dns.icann.org. ... 3600` |
| MX, TXT | mail servers, free text | `example.com. TXT "v=spf1 -all"` |

A delegation is nothing more than NS records in the parent zone. So to find `example.com`'s address, you start at the root, which only knows who runs `com`. You ask `com`, which only knows who runs `example.com`. Then you ask that, and it knows the answer. That's three questions, each to a different organisation. Only a zone's owner can change its records, and nobody else has to be told when it does.

The root itself is served under 13 names, `a.root-servers.net` to `m.root-servers.net`. Each name is many machines around the world that share one address, and the network delivers each packet to the nearest of them (that's called anycast). That makes more than a thousand machines in all, so a root server is never far away. Their addresses are built into the software that does lookups, because nothing can be looked up before them. Next, we'll follow one lookup down this tree, and meet the program that does the walking.

sections.h: Who does the asking: your program, a resolver and three servers
sections.body:
Your program never walks the tree itself. Three kinds of DNS software share the work, and the phone books fit them too.

The **stub resolver** lives inside your program. On Linux it's part of the C library, the basic functions every program can use: `getaddrinfo()`, which Java calls for `InetAddress.getByName`. It reads `/etc/hosts` first, a small file of names and addresses kept on the machine. Then it reads `/etc/resolv.conf` for the address of one recursive resolver. It sends that resolver one question with the RD flag set, a single bit in the message that means recursion desired: "do the whole job for me". Then it waits for the final answer. It keeps no copies itself. In the lab box, the small Linux machine in Docker that this course's Try its use, `/etc/resolv.conf` says `nameserver 127.0.0.11`: Docker's built-in resolver. On a laptop it's usually the home router, the company's resolver, or a public one such as 1.1.1.1.

The **recursive resolver** does the walking, like a directory enquiries service that looks a number up in all the books for you. It sends iterative queries: questions without RD, which every server answers with what it knows. That's either the answer or a referral, "I don't know, but these servers do". The third kind of software, the authoritative servers from the last section, only ever answers for its own zones.

The resolver starts at a root server, and the root answers `example.com A?` with a referral. After the question, every reply has three parts: answers, authority records (who to ask) and additional records (extra help). The root's answer part is empty. Its authority part names the 13 `com` servers, and its additional part gives their addresses. Those addresses are called glue: without them, the resolver would have to look up `a.gtld-servers.net` before it could ask it anything. The `com` server refers it on to example.com's two servers, run by Cloudflare, a company that hosts DNS for many names. One of those answers with the A records and the AA (authoritative answer) flag. The resolver hands the records to the stub with RA (recursion available) set and AA clear, because it's passing on a copy.

Then it keeps everything it learned. The referrals had TTLs of 172,800 seconds, two days. So for two days, this resolver goes straight to the `com` servers and to Cloudflare, and asks the root nothing. The A records had a TTL of 300, so for 5 minutes it answers `example.com` from memory without asking anyone. On a busy resolver, almost every lookup is answered from this cache, its store of saved answers.

All of this travels as UDP datagrams to port 53. UDP sends single packets with no connection, as UDP and the sockets API showed. One question goes in one packet and one answer in another, and the question is sent again after a timeout. An answer too big for one datagram comes back with the TC (truncated) flag, and the resolver asks again over TCP. Step through the whole walk below. Then we'll open one of these messages and read it byte by byte.

aside.title: Why not ask the zone's own server every time?
aside.body: You could, and `dig +trace` does. It costs three round trips, about 110 ms in the Try it, instead of one short trip to a nearby resolver. And every lookup on the internet would start at the root and top-level servers, which could never keep up. Caching is what lets a few root servers answer for everyone. It's also why old answers linger: the two come together.

sections.h: Inside a DNS message: a 12-byte header, the question and the answers
sections.body:
Every DNS message, question or answer, has the same shape. RFC 1035, one of the documents that define DNS, set it in 1987, and every resolver still reads it. This is the whole query `dig` sent for `example.com` in the Try it below: 29 bytes, written in hexadecimal (base 16, two digits per byte).

```text
9984 0100 0001 0000 0000 0000   07 6578616d706c65 03 636f6d 00   0001 0001
header (12 bytes)               e x a m p l e      c o m   end     A    IN
```

The first 12 bytes are the header, six 16-bit numbers. `9984` is the ID, 39300, picked at random by dig. The answer must carry the same ID. Over UDP there's no connection to pair them up, so the ID is how a client matches answers to questions. `0100` holds the flags; only RD is set. Then come four counts: one question, no answers, no authority records, no additional records.

The question is a name, a type and a class. The name travels as labels, each one a length byte and then that many characters: `07 example 03 com 00`. No dots go on the wire, the final zero is the root, and a label can't be longer than 63 bytes. Type `0001` is A, and class `0001` is IN, the internet.

The answer from 1.1.1.1 starts with the same ID. Its flags are `8180`: QR (this is a response), RD copied back, and RA (recursion available). Its counts say one question and two answers. It repeats the question, then gives each answer record as a name, a type (16 bits), a class (16), a TTL (32 bits, in seconds), a data length (16) and the data. An A record's data is the 4-byte address: `ac42 93f3` is 172.66.147.243.

Each answer's name is only two bytes: `c0 0c`. A length byte with its top two bits set isn't a length but a pointer. The other 14 bits are an offset, a position counted from the start of the message: here 12, where the question's name begins. This is **name compression**. The same names repeat all over an answer, and a pointer can replace any ending of a name that appeared earlier. In the CNAME answer the lab reads, `dyna.wikimedia.org` is written as `04 dyna 09 wikimedia`, followed by a pointer to the `org` inside the question. Compression kept answers inside 512 bytes, the old size limit for DNS over UDP.

It also makes parsing, turning the bytes back into fields, a matter of safety. A parser that follows pointers blindly loops forever on a pointer that points to itself, and real DNS software has shipped that bug. The lab's parser follows only pointers that point backwards.

The ID guards against a second danger. Someone who wants to send a program to the wrong address can race the real server with a forged answer. To be accepted, the fake must carry the right ID and reach the right port. Resolvers pick a random source port as well, so a blind forger has to guess about 32 bits, not 16. That makes forging hard, not impossible, and the next lesson adds real proof of who answered. First, though, the TTL field deserves a closer look.

sections.h: Every answer is a copy with an expiry date
sections.body:
A resolver that passes an answer on keeps a copy for as long as the TTL allows, and tells the next client only the time that's left. Ask a busy resolver twice, 16 seconds apart, and the TTL in the answer drops by 16. That one rule explains most DNS surprises.

Nothing is pushed. Say the owner of `ledger.pay.test`, the lab's made-up name for the payments company's accounts computer, changes its address. The authoritative server answers with the new one at once. Every copy already sitting in a cache stays wrong until its own TTL runs out. Different resolvers fetched their copies at different moments, so the world switches over gradually, during one TTL. That spread is all that "DNS propagation" is. With a TTL of 300 it's over in 5 minutes. With 86,400 it takes a day, which is where the "24 to 48 hours" folklore comes from.

In the phone-book picture, the enquiries service writes each number it finds on a card with an expiry date, and reads from the card until that date. Nobody phones it when a number changes.

So plan a move one TTL ahead. A day before, lower the TTL to 60 seconds, because the old, long TTL has to run out everywhere first. Then move, and raise the TTL again. The classic mistake is to change the address and lower the TTL in the same step. Every copy made under the old TTL then lives out its old life. **Nothing tells a cache that a record changed. Shorten the TTL one old TTL before you move.**

A "no" is cached too. If a name doesn't exist, the authoritative server answers NXDOMAIN (non-existent domain, response code 3) and puts its zone's SOA record in the authority section. RFC 2308 says to cache that "no" for the smaller of two numbers: the SOA record's own TTL, and the SOA's minimum field, its last number. For `pay.test` both are 60 seconds; for `iana.org`, 3600. Here's the trap. A setup script looks up a name a few seconds before the record is created, and the resolver caches the NXDOMAIN. The new computer then stays unreachable through that resolver for up to that long after the record exists. A name that exists but has no record of the asked type gets NOERROR (the "all fine" code) with no answers, cached the same way.

The resolver's side of this is a few lines of code: store each answer with "expires at now + TTL", serve it while now is earlier, and report the expiry minus now as the TTL. A CNAME chain, one name pointing to another, is only as fresh as its shortest link. In the Wikipedia answer the lab reads, the CNAME had a day left and the A record 2 seconds, so the whole answer expires in 2. The lab builds this cache.

The Try it below runs an authoritative server for the made-up zone `pay.test` on router, and a caching resolver on peer. Both are about 200 lines of Python in `labs/env/net/dns.py`, because the lab box image has no DNS server software. You change a record at the source and watch the resolver keep the old one until its TTL is up. The resolver isn't the last place a copy hides, though.

sections.h: Two more copies: Java's cache and the open connection
sections.body:
The resolver's cache isn't the last one. Between DNS and a payment sit two more copies, and neither reads the TTL.

Java caches the result of every successful lookup in `InetAddress` for 30 seconds by default, whatever TTL the answer had, and every failed one for 10 seconds. It's your own address book, which you check before you phone enquiries. The settings are the security properties `networkaddress.cache.ttl` and `networkaddress.cache.negative.ttl`. Set them in `$JAVA_HOME/conf/security/java.security`, or with `Security.setProperty` at start-up, before the first lookup. `-Dsun.net.inetaddr.ttl` sets the first one from the command line. 0 turns the cache off, and -1 keeps answers forever. Thirty seconds is a sensible default. A record with a TTL of 5 still costs at most one lookup per 30 seconds per Java program, and a changed record is picked up at most 30 seconds late.

The open connection is the bigger copy, because DNS is asked only when a connection opens. A connection pool (a set of open connections a program keeps and reuses, from TCP connections: handshake, states and TIME_WAIT) may hold a connection to `api.bank.example` that opened at 09:00. It keeps going to the address found at 09:00 for as long as the pool keeps it, whatever DNS says by now. In phone terms, it's a call you never hung up. When the bank moves to a new address and keeps the old one running for a while, the program follows only as its pool replaces connections. That's why connection pools have a maximum connection lifetime, and why the old address finally refusing connections is often what moves a program over.

Linux itself adds no cache. The C library's stub asks the resolver every time, unless the machine runs a local cache such as systemd-resolved or nscd. macOS does cache, in a program called mDNSResponder.

That's the whole answer to the opening's 10:45 puzzle. The resolver kept a copy made under the old TTL, Java added up to 30 seconds, and pooled connections never asked again. Each copy follows its own clock, and that's the limit of DNS: once an answer is out, nobody can reach into the copies and fix them.

try.title: Watch the JVM hold on to an old address
steps: In the lab box, add `ledger.pay.test` to `/etc/hosts`, the first place the stub resolver looks. The `move` function rewrites the file in place: Docker mounts `/etc/hosts` into the container, so `sed -i` can't replace it.
Schedule a move to `.41` in 10 seconds, and run `JvmCache.java`, which looks the name up once a second for 40 seconds and prints a line whenever the answer changes. Predict when Java sees `.41`.
Move it back and run again with `-Dsun.net.inetaddr.ttl=0`, which turns Java's cache off.

From one run:

```text
networkaddress.cache.ttl = null, sun.net.inetaddr.ttl = null
20:50:22  t= 0 s  ledger.pay.test -> 10.10.4.40
20:50:30  /etc/hosts now says 10.10.4.41
20:50:53  t=30 s  ledger.pay.test -> 10.10.4.41
done after 40 s
20:51:04  /etc/hosts now says 10.10.4.40
networkaddress.cache.ttl = null, sun.net.inetaddr.ttl = 0
20:51:06  t= 0 s  ledger.pay.test -> 10.10.4.40
20:51:14  /etc/hosts now says 10.10.4.41
20:51:14  t= 8 s  ledger.pay.test -> 10.10.4.41
```

The file changed 8 seconds into the first run, because Java took about 2 of the 10 seconds to start. Java kept answering `.40` until its 30-second entry expired, 22 seconds after the change. With the cache off it saw the change within the second. `null` means the property isn't set, so the JDK's built-in 30 seconds applies. A hosts file has no TTL at all, which makes Java's own rule easy to see. If Java starts slowly on your machine and the first line already says `.41`, run it again.

compare.title: Asking the authority and asking a resolver

a.label: The authoritative server
a.title: dig @10.10.1.2 ledger.pay.test A +norecurse
a.src:
;; flags: qr aa; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 1, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 0

;; ANSWER SECTION:
ledger.pay.test.	30	IN	A	10.10.4.40

the TTL is always the full 30: this is the original

b.label: The caching resolver
b.title: dig @10.10.1.20 ledger.pay.test A, twice
b.src:
;; flags: qr rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 1, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 0

;; ANSWER SECTION:
ledger.pay.test.	30	IN	A	10.10.4.40      first ask: fetched just now
ledger.pay.test.	24	IN	A	10.10.4.40      5 s later: a copy, 24 s left

compare.note: Both come from the lab network with `env/net/dns.py` running. The flags tell you which kind of answer you have. `aa` means the owner of the zone answered. `ra` without `aa` means a resolver passed on a copy, and its TTL is whatever is left of that copy's life. When you check a DNS change, ask the authoritative server directly (`dig +norecurse @` one of the zone's NS servers) to see the truth, and the resolver to see what your programs see.

worked.title: Read a DNS answer by hand

steps.say: Take the answer frame from the second Try it. The DNS message starts at byte 42 (`0x2a`), after 14 bytes of Ethernet, 20 of IP and 8 of UDP headers. Its first 12 bytes are the DNS header.
steps.code:
0x0020:  0002 0035 b83e 0045 6923 9984 8180 0001
0x0030:  0002 0000 0000 ...

99 84   ID 39300, the same as in the query
81 80   1000 0001 1000 0000: QR=1 (response), RD=1, RA=1, rcode 0 (NOERROR)
00 01   1 question     00 02   2 answers
00 00   0 authority    00 00   0 additional

steps.say: The question follows at offset 12 of the message (12 bytes from its start): the name as labels, then the type and the class. It ends at offset 29.
steps.code:
07 65 78 61 6d 70 6c 65   length 7: "example"
03 63 6f 6d               length 3: "com"
00                        the root: end of the name
00 01   type A    00 01   class IN

steps.say: The first answer record starts at offset 29. Its name is a pointer: `c0` has the top two bits set, and the remaining 14 bits, `00 0c`, are offset 12, where `example.com` already appeared.
steps.code:
c0 0c         pointer to offset 12: "example.com"
00 01         type A
00 01         class IN
00 00 00 1e   TTL 30 seconds
00 04         4 bytes of data
ac 42 93 f3   172.66.147.243

steps.say: The second record has the same shape, with the other address. Add it all up: 12 bytes of header, 17 of question (13 of name, 4 of type and class) and 16 per record. Without compression, each record would carry the 13-byte name instead of a 2-byte pointer.

lab.title: A DNS message codec and a resolver cache
steps: Run the tests once from the `labs` folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All 18 fail for now. `DnsMessage.kt` is finished: the header flags, questions and records as data classes, with each record's data already split by type. The tests read four real frames from `src/test/resources/sfz/net/l09/`: the query and answer from the second Try it, a CNAME answer and an NXDOMAIN.
In `DnsCodec.kt` (a codec turns messages into bytes and back), write `encodeName` and `encodeQuery`. The test compares your query with dig's, byte for byte.

Write `readName`: labels until the zero byte, following pointers, but only backwards. Then write `decode`: the header, the questions, then the three record lists, with each record's data decoded by its type.

In `ResolverCache.kt`, write `put` and `get` with the rules from the fourth section: the smallest TTL for an answer, `min(SOA TTL, SOA minimum)` for a "no", and nothing for errors. `ResolverCacheTest` moves a `ManualClock` instead of sleeping. Run the tests until all 18 pass.
hints: `ByteBuffer.allocate(n).putShort(id.toShort())...array()` builds the query: 12 bytes of header, plus the encoded name, plus 4.
In `readName`, remember where the name ended in the place you started: the first pointer you meet ends it 2 bytes after the pointer. Keep that, however many jumps follow.
A pointer is `((len and 0x3f) shl 8) or nextByte`. Check `target < at` before you jump; that one check stops every loop.

Read TTLs and SOA numbers as numbers that can't be negative: `getInt(at).toLong() and 0xFFFF_FFFFL`. After decoding a record's data, move on by RDLENGTH (the data length field), not by what you read: a compressed name inside the data is shorter than the name it stands for.
In the cache, key on `name.lowercase()` and the type. Store the absolute expiry, `clock() + seconds * 1000`; `get` divides what is left by 1000 for whole seconds.

drill.title: Write readName from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write `readName(msg: ByteArray, offset: Int): Pair<String, Int>`. It reads a DNS name, possibly compressed, starting at `offset`, and returns it with the offset right after the name in the place where you started. Follow pointers, and refuse any pointer that doesn't point backwards. Then say in one sentence why the returned offset isn't where the last label ended.

recap: Names form a tree of zones. Each zone hands its children to their own servers with NS records, and only a zone's authoritative servers hold the originals. The root knows only who runs each top-level domain.

Your program's stub resolver asks one recursive resolver to do the whole job (RD set). The resolver walks root, top-level and authoritative servers with iterative queries, following referrals and glue, and caches everything it learns.

A DNS message is a 12-byte header (ID, flags, four counts), the question, then answer, authority and additional records. Names are labels with a length byte each, and `c0 0c` points back to offset 12.
Every copy lives for its TTL and nothing is pushed: "propagation" is copies running out. A "no" (NXDOMAIN) is cached for min(SOA TTL, SOA minimum).
Java caches lookups for 30 s (failures for 10 s) whatever the TTL, and pooled connections keep the address they opened with. Lower TTLs before a move, and give pools a maximum lifetime.

The limit: once an answer is out, nobody can recall it, and a forged answer with the right ID and port is accepted like a real one. DNS can tell a program where to go, but not prove who answered there.
closing:
We started with payments still going to the bank's old address 45 minutes after it moved. Nothing was broken. The company's resolver held a copy made under a one-hour TTL, Java kept its own for 30 seconds, and pooled connections never asked again.

Try `dig example.com` twice, a few seconds apart, and watch the TTL count down: that's a resolver's copy ageing. Then `dig +norecurse @hera.ns.cloudflare.com example.com` asks one of the zone's own servers for the original.

Next, we'll make sure the computer at that address really is the bank, and lock the connection so that nobody on the way can read or change what it carries.

quiz.q: A resolver with an empty cache gets a query for `api.bank.example` from the payments program. At the least, which servers must it ask?
options: Only the authoritative server for bank.example, which it finds by asking every machine on the network
A root server, a server for the name's top-level domain, then the zone's authoritative server
Only a root server, which knows every name
The top-level domain's server and the authoritative server; root servers are only for top-level names
quiz.why: With nothing cached, the resolver starts from the root addresses built into it. The root refers it to the top-level domain's servers, those refer it to the zone's servers, and those answer. The root never knows individual names, and nothing in DNS is found by asking everyone. With a warm cache, the resolver skips the steps whose referrals it still holds, which is what the fourth option half-remembers.

quiz.q: A setup script runs `dig new-api.pay.example` 10 seconds before the record is created. The zone's SOA record has a TTL of 3600 and a minimum field of 300. For how long after its lookup can the company resolver keep answering NXDOMAIN?
options: 10 seconds, until the record is created
3600 seconds, the SOA record's TTL
Up to 300 seconds, the smaller of the SOA's TTL and its minimum
Until the resolver restarts
quiz.why: RFC 2308 caches a negative answer for min(SOA TTL, SOA minimum), here 300 seconds. Creating the record changes nothing for copies already cached, because nobody tells the resolver. 3600 is tempting because it's the SOA record's own TTL, but the minimum field caps the time a "no" is kept.

quiz.q: A Java program uses the JDK's default DNS settings. The bank's record has a TTL of 5 seconds and moves from address A to address B. The company's resolver respects TTLs. When does a new connection from that program go to B, at the latest?
options: About 35 seconds after the move: up to 5 s in the resolver plus up to 30 s in Java's cache
5 seconds after the move
Immediately: a 5-second TTL turns caching off
Never, until the program restarts
quiz.why: Java caches every successful lookup for 30 seconds whatever the record's TTL, and the lookup it makes after that can still get the last 5 seconds of the resolver's old copy. "Never" is what `networkaddress.cache.ttl=-1` would give you. Connections already open in a pool are a separate matter: they keep using A until the pool closes them.

quiz.q: In a captured DNS answer, the two bytes `c0 0c` stand where a record's name should be. What do they mean?
options: A label of 192 characters follows
Class IN, type 12
The end of the name
A pointer: the name is the one at offset 12 of the message, the question's name
quiz.why: A length byte with its top two bits set is a compression pointer, and the other 14 bits are an offset from the start of the message. Labels can't be longer than 63 bytes precisely so that those two bits are free for this. The end of a name is a single zero byte.

quiz.q: UDP and the sockets API showed dig resending queries over a link that loses packets. Two replies to the same question may then arrive, and a forged reply could arrive too. What lets the client match a reply to its question, and what makes forging one harder?
options: The UDP checksum; nothing protects against forgery
The 16-bit ID copied from the query, together with the client's random source port: a forger has to guess both
The TTL in each record
A sequence number in the UDP header, like TCP's
quiz.why: UDP has no connection and no sequence numbers, so DNS puts its own 16-bit ID in the header, and a reply must echo it. Resolvers also pick a random source port, so a blind attacker has to guess about 32 bits, not 16. The checksum only catches damage on the way, and the TTL says how long to keep an answer, not which question it answers.

flashcards.front: What does a root server answer to `example.com A?`
flashcards.back: A referral: the com servers' NS records, plus their addresses as glue. It never knows example.com's address.

flashcards.front: Stub resolver or recursive resolver: what does each do?
flashcards.back: The stub lives in your program (the C library's getaddrinfo), asks one resolver with RD set, and keeps no copies. The recursive resolver walks the root, top-level and authoritative servers, and caches what it learns.
How many seconds a copy may be kept. Each cache counts it down and passes on only what's left. Nothing is pushed when the record changes.

flashcards.front: How long is a "no such name" (NXDOMAIN) cached?
flashcards.back: min(SOA record's TTL, SOA minimum field), from the SOA in the authority section (RFC 2308).

flashcards.front: What are Java's DNS cache defaults?
flashcards.back: 30 s for answers and 10 s for failures, whatever the TTL: `networkaddress.cache.ttl` and `networkaddress.cache.negative.ttl`.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't a DNS change move a pooled connection?
flashcards.back: DNS is only asked when a connection opens. A pooled connection keeps its address until the pool closes it.

flashcards.front: What do the flags `aa` and `ra` tell you in dig's output?
flashcards.back: `aa`: the zone's own server answered, so it's an original. `ra` without `aa`: a resolver answered from its copy.

terms.plain: A piece of the name tree run by one owner and served by its authoritative servers.
NS records in a parent zone that hand a child zone to other servers.
A server that holds a zone's original records and sets the AA flag in its answers.
The server that walks the tree for a program and keeps copies of the answers.
The small resolver inside your program that asks one recursive resolver and waits.
The addresses of a child zone's name servers, sent along with a referral.
Time to live: the number of seconds a copy of a record may be kept.
Keeping a "no such name" answer, for the SOA's minimum or its TTL, whichever is smaller.

explain_back.prompt: The bank's technical team says: "We moved api.bank.example to the new address an hour ago, DNS has propagated, so why are you still calling the old one?" Explain to them what happens between their authoritative server and your payments program, which copies are involved, and what you'd check and change.
explain_back.answer: Nothing in DNS spreads outward. Your authoritative server answered with the new address the moment you changed it. But every resolver that copied the old record keeps its copy until its TTL runs out. If the old TTL was a day, our company's resolver can serve the old address for up to a day after the change. On our side there are two more copies. Java keeps every lookup for 30 seconds by default, which only adds a little. The bigger one is our connection pool: DNS is only asked when a connection opens, so connections opened before the change keep going to the old address until the pool closes them. I'd check what our resolver returns and the TTL it shows, compare that with `dig +norecurse` against your authoritative servers, and look at our pool's maximum connection lifetime. Next time, I'd ask you to lower the TTL to a minute a day before the move, and we'd make sure the pool replaces its connections within a few minutes.

deeper.body:
**DNSSEC.** Run `dig +trace` without `+nodnssec`, and you see DS and RRSIG records at every step. With DNSSEC, each zone signs its records, and the parent vouches for the child's key with a DS record: a chain of trust up to the root's key, which validating resolvers have built in. It proves an answer came from the zone's owner and wasn't changed. It doesn't encrypt anything, so anyone on the path can still read which names you ask for.

**Encrypted DNS.** DNS over TLS (RFC 7858, port 853), over HTTPS (RFC 8484) and over QUIC (RFC 9250) encrypt the hop between a client and its resolver, so the network in between can't read or change the questions. Browsers often use DNS over HTTPS directly. A Java program still uses the operating system's plain UDP stub, unless the machine runs a local resolver that forwards over TLS.

**Bigger answers.** RFC 1035 capped UDP answers at 512 bytes. EDNS (the extra record `+noedns` switched off) lets a client announce a bigger buffer. Since DNS Flag Day 2020, resolvers use 1,232 bytes, so answers fit in an IPv6 packet without being split. Anything bigger is truncated (the TC flag) and asked again over TCP. A firewall that blocks TCP port 53 therefore breaks only big answers, which makes it hard to spot.

**A lost question costs seconds.** Lookups go over UDP, and the C library's stub waits 5 seconds before it asks again. So one lost DNS packet adds 5 seconds to the first call after Java's cache runs out, which looks like a slow server rather than a slow lookup.

**ndots in Kubernetes.** Kubernetes, a system that runs programs in containers across many machines, gives each container a `/etc/resolv.conf` that usually says `options ndots:5`, plus several search domains (endings to try). A name with fewer than five dots, such as `api.bank.example`, is first tried with each search domain added (`api.bank.example.default.svc.cluster.local` and so on). So one lookup can become several queries and several NXDOMAINs. A trailing dot (`api.bank.example.`) or a lower `ndots` avoids it.

**Not every "no" is NXDOMAIN.** Some DNS providers answer a query for a name that doesn't exist with NOERROR and no records, instead of NXDOMAIN. example.com's servers did that for `nosuchhost-4242.example.com` while this lesson was written. Resolvers cache both kinds of "no" the same way, by the SOA.
